faq.a: It distinguishes underproduction (low retic) from loss or destruction, pointing to marrow failure.
Most patients require lifelong therapy; HSCT offers cure but is limited by donor availability and resources.
faq.q: Can DBA be cured without HSCT?

faq.a: They can increase residual erythropoiesis in ~ 30 % of patients, delaying or avoiding transfusion dependence.
faq.q: What is the role of steroids?

exam: A 6‑month‑old infant presents with pallor and macrocytic anaemia; bone‑marrow shows absent erythroid precursors. What is the most likely diagnosis and why? — Diamond‑Blackfan anaemia; isolated red‑cell aplasia, macrocytosis, low retic.
How would you differentiate DBA from transient erythroblastopenia of childhood? — Duration (DBA chronic), congenital anomalies, marrow findings, need for steroids/transfusion.
A child with known DBA is now requiring weekly transfusions. What complication must you screen for and how? — Iron overload; check serum ferritin >1000 µg/L and start chelation.
What is the first‑line pharmacologic therapy for DBA and what monitoring is required? — Prednisone; monitor blood pressure, glucose, and response after 8 weeks.
In a low‑resource hospital without genetic testing, which clinical features help you confirm DBA? — Macrocytic anaemia, retic <1 %, congenital anomalies, marrow erythroid hypoplasia.
A patient with DBA develops fever and sudden drop in Hb; what urgent investigation is needed? — Parvovirus B19 PCR/IgM; acute infection can cause aplastic crisis.
Why is HSCT not always the immediate choice for DBA in East Africa? — Limited donor registries, high infection risk, need for intensive supportive care.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt immediate referral to a tertiary centre? — Signs of high‑output cardiac failure or severe iron overload.
ai.title: Diamond-Blackfan Anaemia
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Diamond-Blackfan anaemia (DBA) is a congenital pure red‑cell aplasia presenting in infancy with macrocytic anaemia, low reticulocytes and often physical anomalies. Diagnosis relies on blood film, marrow findings and exclusion of other causes.

b: Bone‑marrow: <5 % erythroid precursors, normal myeloid and megakaryocytic lines
sections.p: DBA is a rare inherited disorder of erythropoiesis characterised by failure of red‑cell precursors, leading to macrocytic anaemia with a reticulocyte count <1 %. Diagnosis requires a peripheral smear, bone‑marrow biopsy showing paucity of erythroid precursors, and exclusion of other causes of normocytic or macrocytic anaemia.

t.b: Is there anaemia and what is the red cell size? Low Hb with MCV >100 fL suggests macrocytic anaemia.
Is marrow production adequate? <1 % indicates underproduction.
Are red cells macrocytic with anisopoikilocytosis? Confirms macrocytosis, looks for nucleated RBCs.
Is erythropoiesis reduced? <5 % erythroid precursors confirms pure red‑cell aplasia.
Does the patient have a known DBA mutation? Positive result supports diagnosis; unavailable? rely on clinical criteria.

b: Severe: Hb < 7 g/dL or chronic transfusion
sections.p: Severity is graded by transfusion dependence and haemoglobin level. The International DBA Registry uses three grades: mild (Hb ≥ 9 g/dL, no transfusion), moderate (Hb 7‑9 g/dL, occasional transfusion), severe (Hb < 7 g/dL or regular transfusion).

b: Inherited ribosomal protein mutations (RPS19, RPL5, RPL11…)
sections.p: Most DBA cases are due to ribosomal protein gene mutations (≈ 70 %). In low‑resource settings, secondary pure red‑cell aplasia from parvovirus B19 infection must be considered, especially in children with sickle cell disease or HIV.

Infants present with pallor, poor feeding, tachycardia and growth failure. Physical anomalies occur in ~ 50 % (triphalangeal thumbs, craniofacial dysmorphism, cardiac defects). In low‑resource settings, presentation may be delayed until severe anaemia forces presentation.
Focus on confirming pure red‑cell aplasia, ruling out infection, and identifying associated anomalies.

t.b: Is the anaemia infection‑related? Positive IgM indicates acute B19 infection, treat supportively.
Is HIV contributing? Positive test prompts antiretroviral review and infection control.
Are there structural heart defects? Detects VSD, ASD that may need referral.
Any renal anomaly? Guides multidisciplinary care.
Is iron overload present from transfusions? Elevated ferritin >1000 µg/L indicates need for chelation.

sections.p: Untreated severe anaemia can cause high‑output cardiac failure. Chronic transfusion leads to iron overload, endocrine dysfunction, and liver disease. There is an increased risk of malignancy (especially AML).

b: If no response after 8 weeks, start regular packed RBC transfusion (aim Hb > 9 g/dL).
Deferoxamine or deferasirox for ferritin > 1000 µg/L – prevents organ damage.
HSCT for severe, steroid‑refractory cases – curative but requires donor and supportive care.
sections.p: Initial management aims to stabilise anaemia, then address the underlying defect. Corticosteroids are first‑line; if ineffective, consider chronic transfusion with iron chelation. In selected patients, hematopoietic stem‑cell transplantation (HSCT) offers cure.

b: Hb and reticulocyte count every 3 months
Ferritin every 6 months; start chelation if >1000 µg/L
Annual cardiac echo if transfusion dependent
Growth chart review at each clinic visit
sections.p: Regular monitoring of haemoglobin, growth, cardiac status and iron load is essential. Vaccination against parvovirus B19 is not available; educate families on infection avoidance and prompt treatment of febrile illnesses.

b: Aplastic anaemia (pancytopenia, not isolated red‑cell line)
sections.p: Conditions that also cause macrocytic anaemia with low reticulocytes.

b: Normal MCV early in disease – do not rule out DBA
Transient rise in reticulocytes after infection – re‑check after 2 weeks
sections.p: In early disease, reticulocyte count may be borderline, and marrow may appear normal; reliance on a single smear can miss subtle erythroid hypoplasia.

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of cardiac failure (tachypnoea, edema, hepatomegaly)
